# **‐ Copper Supply Constraints Coming on Stream: 2009 2012 and Beyond Executive Summary** - Historically, refined copper prices have been kept under control by **increasing amounts of mine supply** associated to technology improvements. The fast reaction capacity of the copper recycling industry to the higher refined copper prices is a buffer to avoid long and extreme price volatility. The world faced a huge expansion in copper manufacturing capacity and production in China, and a heavy contraction **i** n en **d** copper use outs **id** e **Chi** na. **Chi** nese copper usage an **d** stoc **k** p **ili** ng **h** as **b** een res **ili** ent an **d** t **h** e supp y **l** o **f** copper **f** or **l** ong term grow ng **i** Chinese demands raises some challenges. Global copper demand is expected to recover sustainably with the industrial product

ion in years to come. 

- **Economic risks affecting future copper mine supply** are growing. Now the industry is looking at high capital costs *lack of project funds* in **copper exploration** , **mining** , **smelting and refining** . **Capital cost overruns in copper projects are also a concern** , **caused by unexpected inflation** , contractor negotiations, labour strikes, use of market power by copper users or producers, and changes in copper industry ownership structure. Changes in mining taxation and investment regimes can delay invests in copper industry in promising regions as RDC, Mongolia and others . Other variables, as the cost of keeping peace and security in post conflict countries with high geological endowments of copper, based in current costs of ongoing peace keeping missions are included in the report. 

- **Internal risks of supply constraints** caused market bottlenecks in recent years and will increase with falling investment flows to copper mine projects. Constraints on power supply, volatile shipping costs, skilled workers, inputs and machinery are adding to geologic and maintenance limits. Copper supply is now more sensitive to local sulphuric acid market balance affecting SX‐EW plants. International labour mobility restrictions may reduce labour market forces to balance skilled workers demand, nevertheless other variables as falling copper ore grades in high scale mining regions and the lack of water are constraints harder to manage specially in a world with restricted credit. Base metals markets as copper may exper ence **i severe availability bottlenecks and price volatility if** some o **f th** e supp y cons **l t** ra n **i t** s men **ti** one **d** a **b** ove are co nc **i id** en **t** with a stronger demand for copper intensive products coming from the developing world and from an eventual OECD recovery in the next five years. 



- The research on supply constraints has been enriched by the document on investment legislation and tax regimes of James Otto: Also by recently **published research of Lagos** , **Jara &Tilton** , **on the role of exploration expenditure in mining investment climate** . **LATAM Latin American Mining** Conference allowed ICSG to obtain the most recent estimations on **exploration budgets** 2008‐2009 from the industry, and to include the views of World Bank Group, International Financial Corporation and United States agencies on activities supporting mining supply. The Framework for Analyzing the Impacts of Investment Legislation and Tax Regimes on Global Copper Supply Coming on Stream (Otto 2009) found that **geological endowment has been the main driver of copper mine investments included in ICSG Directory of Capacity of Copper Mines and Plants.** Indexes of perception of mineral potential indexes, considering changes in investment and tax regimes to assess mineral investment c imate are not re ate **l l d** to past c **h** anges in copper capacity in **d** exes.

Copper first use and the subsequent **investments in copper mines will not rebound before a sustained growth of industrial production.** **2. Capital Cost Impact on Technology Choice.** Low or subsidized capital cost increase the choice of highly capital intensive technology. Higher financial cost of capital incentive less capital intense copper production techniques. **3. Capital Cost Impact on Copper Project Power Supply.** When financial cost of capital is high, electricity generation based on capital intensive options (distant hydro dams or nuclear power plants) is less attractive than oil or coal plants. **4. Capital Cost Impact on Project Scale.** The scale of projects is constrained by technological factors, but optimal scale will be lower if capital is less available. **5. Project Capital Spending and Industry Concentration** . Large copper corporations with low debt will likely look to continue investing in their project pipeline. Smaller low debt mining corporations may be engaged in more merger and acquisitions. **6. Capital Cost Impact on Investment Timing** . **A copper mine or plant built too soon in the** cycle could result in a large amount of overcapacity. **7. Citigroup Metal Report. Medium and long term fundamentals of the copper market likely to be dominated by supply side issues: new 18 copper mine projects adding 4.7** **Mt‐cu to 2020 supply, but doubts of the commercial viability of many of these projects** financing
### **Capital Cost Overruns in Copper Mining: Net benefits of the mining projects tend to be overestimated to secure financing** - Review of 63 international mining and smelting projects (Colorado School of Mines **2008):** - feasibility studies tend to underestimate on average 25% in nominal terms (14% in real terms) the effective capital costs of the projects. - Feasibility studies of large projects are more accurate when compared to studies of smaller projects. - Conclusion: net financial benefits of the mining projects tend to be overestimated to secure financing. In a situation of less capital available there will be a trend to inflate project net benefits even more. - There could be a need for more information on the past performance on cost of capital estimations: - **for consulting engineering firms** - , - for construction firms contracting copper mining / metallurgy projects. - The Secretariat will examine the possibility of further work in this area. #

## **What we Know About Strike Prevention in the Copper Industry?** - Card, 1988 - Strike duration negatively correlated with industry output. - The probability of strike increases when industry product prices increase. - **Strike probability falls when unemployment increases** - . - Cramton and Tracy, 2003 - Strike incidence is generally found to be pro‐cyclical: more strikes when the economy is good and vice versa. - Strike duration moves against the cycle: strikes are longer when the economy is weak. - Conclusion: some of the findings in strike research valid for the copper industry, - There is not any published copper industry specific analysis of the economic determinants . - **and the empiric analysis of copper strikes in the last 30 years** - The Secretariat will examine the possibility of further work in this area. ### **The Strategic Role of Water Management in Dry Copper Mining Ecosystems** **_Water resources in dry mining areas_ key topic due to: importance of water in economic activity, environment and quality of life.** **Situation:** **limited availability, growing demand and competition with other sectors** . **of the economy** **In deposits located in uninhabited dry areas and extreme climates, water becomes a critical and even strategic component.** #### **COCHILCO: Good Practices and Efficient Use of Water in the Mining Industry in Chile** o **1.
